items.title: David Brinkley Interview, 1962-01-10
items.q: a young couple named Alan and Sandra Jaffe started this.

ctx.x: Well, there were times that we put the music above the ring of the cash register, the tinkle of the ice and the glasses. There were many times, one in particular, when Papa Celestan played, he did a thing called Just Telephone Me with a tight mute in it. And no one served a drink, and the register didn't ring, and no one spoke, said a word. It was just about the same as being in the cathedral at high mass. We wanted the real thing, the genuine thing, and that's what we kept here for four or five years. The time…

New Orleans people, of course, are aware their jazz heritage is disappearing, and some are trying somehow to save the only art form that is strictly, entirely American. One effort to save it is here at Preservation Hall. An art dealer named Larry Borenstein furnished the hall, and a young couple named Alan and Sandra Jaffe started this. Six nights a week, jazz bands play here in the traditional style they like. There are no drinks and no strippers. Here's Jaffe.

Jazz here in Bourbon Street is what people seem to think is going to sell drinks. What we're trying to do here is just present the music the way the men want to play it. The people are sitting on wooden benches, sitting on the floor. There's no drinks. It's pretty hot in there too in the summer. People come to hear just the music. I think the men realize this.
